plain_claim: (i) In a single interpreted world over the parameter values 0..7, with atom 0 read as "divisible by 4" and atom 1 as "even" (a single world, so the empty report already decides every claim): "divisible by 4 gives even" holds, "divisible by 4 is needed for evenness" is false, the hypothesis is tight for "under divisibility by 4, even" (1 is neither), and the exhaustified reading of that claim under the standard alternatives holds. (ii) In the 16-world space S22, the consistent report E_tight (∀x, A⇒B; ∃x, B∧¬A; ∃x, ¬A∧¬B) proves ∀x, A⇒B, proves that A is tight for it (which the empty report does not), and entails its exhaustified reading, yet contradicts "A is needed for B". In both instances the hypothesis is sufficient and tight, and "needed" is false.
nonvacuity_witness: The instances themselves.
non_claims: Instance (i) uses a single-world space: entailment collapses to truth in that world (the empty report entails every true claim), no claim is open (`interp_never_open`), every literally safe rendering is strengthening-safe with no flags (`interp_literallySafe_strengtheningSafe_unblocked`), and exhaustification excludes ∀x, even because it is false in that world, not because it is open. Instance (ii) is the multi-world counterpart.

`tightFor H C` (∃x, ¬H ∧ ¬C) models tightness of a single hypothesis H in ∀x, H ⇒ C; for ∀x, (H₁ ∧ H₂) ⇒ C, tightness of H₁ also requires H₂ at the witness, which is not modeled. `tightFor` does not check that the theorem itself holds (`tightFor_does_not_check_theorem`).

These are statements about a toy model: finitely many listed worlds, uninterpreted atoms over a finite parameter list, a single bound variable (inner quantifiers shadow outer ones), material implication for both `→` and `⇒`, and three stated reader rules applied deterministically. They neither establish nor refute the corresponding claims about how actual readers interpret actual summary sentences; any such connection is a separate `derived (modeling bridge)` claim, resting on experimental work such as Noveck (2001; Cognition 78(2):165-188, doi:10.1016/S0010-0277(00)00114-1) and Bott and Noveck (2004; Journal of Memory and Language 51(3):437-457, doi:10.1016/j.jml.2004.05.006), which find that adults often, though not always, read "some" as "some but not all" and that this reading takes extra processing time.
prior_art: K. von Fintel, "Conditional strengthening: A case study in implicature", unpublished manuscript, MIT, draft version of 13 September 2001, https://web.mit.edu/fintel/fintel-2001-condstrength.pdf (no DOI). Section "Not True No Matter What" (pp. 5-8): the quantity implicature of "if p, q" against the competitor "q no matter what" is that q is not unconditionally true; p. 8 stresses that this is much weaker than the claim that the antecedent is a necessary condition. This is the gap between tightness (an existential counterexample) and necessity modeled here.

M. L. Geis and A. M. Zwicky, "On invited inferences", Linguistic Inquiry 2(4):561-566, 1971. Names the invited inference of conditional perfection ("If you mow the lawn, I'll give you five dollars" invites "if not, not").

L. R. Horn, "From if to iff: Conditional perfection as pragmatic strengthening", Journal of Pragmatics 32(3):289-326, 2000, doi:10.1016/S0378-2166(99)00053-3. Analyzes conditional perfection as pragmatic strengthening.
design_question: May a report write "H is needed" for a hypothesis it has shown to be tight? (Not in general: in both instances the hypothesis is tight yet "needed" is false; tightness is existential, necessity is universal.)

tier_justification: Folklore about reading "not shown" as "false", made precise.
plain_claim: For every finite space S, report E and claim c: (a) if the disclaimer "c is not shown" is true (E ⊭ c), then the reader rule "not shown ↦ false" makes it unsafe iff E leaves c open (neither proves nor refutes c); (b) the blocked disclaimer "c is not shown, and not refuted" is safe iff E leaves c open.

hypotheses.name: htrue : DisclaimerTrue S E (.notShown c)
hypotheses.purpose: statement (a): DisclaimerSafe requires the disclaimer to be true (definition), so a false disclaimer is unsafe even when c is not open
hypotheses.witness_class: the 4-world space S21 with report [p0], which proves c = p0 and makes the disclaimer false

nonvacuity_witness: S21, E = [], c = p0: the bare disclaimer is true and unsafe, c is open, the blocked disclaimer is safe.
non_claims: When E refutes c the "false" reading is safe (`not_shown_read_as_false_safe_when_refuted`); the result does not say disclaimers are always misread.

`Open S E c` is semantic independence of c from E over the listed worlds (a world satisfying E and ¬c, and one satisfying E and c); it does not license writing "not shown, and not refuted" when c was merely not examined and E might entail ¬c.

`disclaimerReadings` fixes the readings by definition ("not shown" ↦ ¬c; the blocked form ↦ nothing); neither the "not shown ↦ false" inference nor its blocking is derived from exhaustification, the alternatives or the cancellation filter.
Disclaimers are statements about E; their truth is not a property of worlds.

design_question: How should a report state that something is not established without being read as refuting it? (Under this model, "not shown, and not refuted" is safe exactly when the matter is open; this requires checking that the report neither proves nor refutes it, not merely that it was not examined.)

tier_justification: The clash between perfection (if ↦ iff) and a scalar reading of if against the stronger iff (if ↦ merely sufficient) is noted in the conditional-perfection literature (von Fintel 2001 ms., pp. 13-14); the impossibility for a consistent report and the blocker characterization are precise formulations of it.
plain_claim: For the one-step reader `readings` with the standard alternatives `stdAlt`, every finite space S, report E and claims a, b: (a) if E is consistent, ∀x, a→b is consistent with its perfected reading ∀x, a↔b (PerfectionConsistent S a b), and ∀x, a→b is consistent with ¬∀x, b→a (ConverseExcludable S a b), then the rendering ∀x, a→b is not strengthening-safe for E without blocker flags; (b) if in addition E ⊨ ∀x, a→b, then its computed blocker set is {perfection} if E refutes ∀x, b→a, {exhaustification} if E proves ∀x, b→a, and {perfection, exhaustification} if E does neither; (c) if PerfectionConsistent S a b and E leaves ∀x, b→a open, then its computed blocker set is {perfection, exhaustification}.

hypotheses.name: hE : Sat S E
hypotheses.purpose: statements (a), (b): an inconsistent report entails every reading
hypotheses.witness_class: the 16-world space S22 with a = A, b = B and the inconsistent report [p0, ¬p0]

hypotheses.name: hlit : LiterallySafe S E (∀x, a→b)
hypotheses.purpose: statement (b): the exhaustified reading has the rendering as a conjunct (definition of exh), so a report that does not prove the rendering does not entail it, and the blocker set can differ from the one stated; instance in the counterexample
hypotheses.witness_class: the 16-world space S22 with a = A, b = B and the report [¬∀x, B→A]

hypotheses.name: hperf : PerfectionConsistent S a b
hypotheses.purpose: statements (a), (b), (c): without it the perfected reading ∀x, a↔b is inconsistent with the rendering and is cancelled (definition of ruleReadings)
hypotheses.witness_class: (a) the 2-world space disagreeSpace (atoms 0 and 1 always disagree; not a full valuation space) with report [∀x, A→B], and the full 4-world space S12 with b = ¬a and report [∀x, A→¬A]; (b) disagreeSpace with E_notConv; (c) disagreeSpace with the empty report

hypotheses.name: hconv : ConverseExcludable S a b
hypotheses.purpose: statements (a), (b): without it ∀x, a→b entails its converse over the listed worlds, so the converse is not available for exclusion; in the counterexample exhaustification adds nothing and the unflagged rendering is safe
hypotheses.witness_class: the 4-world space S12 with a = b = A and the empty report

hypotheses.name: hopen : Open S E (∀x, b→a)
hypotheses.purpose: statement (c): a report that refutes the converse can have a one-flag blocker set (in the counterexample it is {perfection}; compare statement (b))
hypotheses.witness_class: the 16-world space S22 with a = A, b = B and E_notConv, which refutes the converse

nonvacuity_witness: S22 with a = A, b = B: E_notConv satisfies the hypotheses of (a) and of (b) (refuted branch); [∀x, A↔B] and [∀x, A→B] satisfy those of (b) (proved and open branches); [∀x, A→B] satisfies those of (c).
non_claims: Escape hatches depend on what E proves about the converse (statement (b)): if E refutes ∀x, b→a, the perfection flag alone restores safety, and so does the rendering "(∀x, a→b) ∧ ¬(∀x, b→a)" in the instance of dropping-a-blocking-conjunct-breaks-strengthening-safety; if E proves ∀x, b→a, the exhaustification flag alone restores safety; if E leaves ∀x, b→a open, neither "iff" nor "and not conversely" is literally safe (`open_converse_rewordings_not_literally_safe`), and, for a report proving ∀x, a→b with PerfectionConsistent S a b, a flag set is safe iff it contains both the perfection and the exhaustification flags (`forall_conditional_open_converse_safe_iff_both_flags`; instances in `forall_conditional_safe_with_blockers`).

The perfection flag alone does not express "the converse is open": with that flag alone, exhaustification still negates the converse whenever the converse is innocently excludable (`forall_conditional_safe_with_blockers`, open-converse instance).

In the full valuation spaces S22 and S32 the distinct atoms A, B satisfy both PerfectionConsistent and ConverseExcludable (`distinct_atoms_nondegenerate_in_full_spaces`); the counterexamples for hperf and hconv use a restricted space, b = ¬a, or a = b.

For a quantifier-free single-value conditional such as p0 → q0, neighbouring-value alternatives add further exhaustified content: even when the report refutes q0 → p0 in S22, the perfection flag alone is not enough (`single_value_conditional_needs_exhaustification_flag`).

Depends on the standard alternatives (converse and biconditional of a conditional): with alternative antecedents instead, exhaustification may agree with perfection (not proved here); nothing is claimed for that reader, either way.

design_question: Can a bare "A gives B" headline be safe against both default readers? (Under this reader model, not without flags when the report is consistent and both PerfectionConsistent and ConverseExcludable hold; which flags suffice depends on whether the report refutes, proves, or leaves open the converse; for a report that proves ∀x, a→b and leaves the converse open, with PerfectionConsistent S a b, a flag set is safe iff it contains both the perfection and the exhaustification flags.)
